# Tidyup 10: R virtual environments (`rig proj` / `.rvenv`)

**Champion**: Gábor Csárdi

**Co-champion**: TBD

**Status**: Draft

## Abstract

R has no equivalent of Python's `venv`: a per-project, isolated
package library, tied to a specific R version, plus a matching activation
solution that works the same way across shells, scripts, CI and IDEs.
renv is the closest existing tool, but it predates R-installation managers
like `rig`, isolates only packages rather than pinning R itself, and
activates by shadowing the user's `.Rprofile`, which causes real,
frequently-reported problems.

This tidyup proposes a from-scratch, user-space R virtual environment
design (`.rvenv`), built without modifying R itself, and its integration
into `rig` as `rig proj lock`/`sync`/`rig run`. It brings R up to the
level `uv` set for Python: a venv pinned to an exact R version and
platform, three independent activation layers (a shell wrapper, an
implicit `rig run` layer for scripts/CI, and a tracked `.Renviron` +
shim package for IDEs) instead of a project `.Rprofile`, and a
content-addressed package store shared with `rig`'s existing install
machinery. None of the three activation layers shadows the user's own R
configuration.

## Motivation

R lacks the tooling picture Python has built up around `venv`/`uv`.
Most importantly:

- No way to pin and manage the R installation itself alongside a project's
  packages, the way `uv` pins an interpreter version next to its packages.
  renv isolates only packages, predates R-installation managers like
  `rig`, and has no notion of "this project needs R 4.3.2."
- No standard notion of a project-local package library that "just works"
  across shells, scripts, CI and IDEs at once.
- No wrapper/shim convention analogous to a venv's `bin/python`, so
  activating a project environment for interactive shell use,
  non-interactive scripts, and IDE-launched sessions all require different
  mechanisms today, if they exist at all.

## Solution

We propose `.rvenv`, a per-project R environment directory, built entirely
in user space.

### Layout

```
project-root/
  rproj.lock              # tracked, lock file (see Tidyup 9 for the manifest side)
  .Renviron               # tracked, IDE-activation leg
  .gitignore              # tracked, /.rvenv/
  .rvenvlib/
    rvenv/                # tracked, minimal shim package, written by init
  .rvenv/
    lib/...               # untracked, the project library, filled by sync
    lib/.synced           # untracked, stamp file written by sync (copy of rproj.lock)
    rvenv.cfg             # untracked, machine-specific: R version/minor/platform/arch
    onload.R              # untracked, rest of the shim's .onLoad(), rewritten by sync
    bin/{R,Rscript,...}   # untracked, wrapper scripts, absolute real-R path
    bin/activate{,.fish,.csh}, Activate.ps1
```

`.rvenvlib` is the venv's own half: rig's files, kept out of the project
library so that `.rvenv/lib` holds nothing but the project's packages. It
holds a single library, containing only the shim package, and it is the
only tracked piece of the whole scheme. `.rvenv` itself holds nothing
tracked, so it is fully disposable, `rm -rf .rvenv` and `sync` rebuilds it.
The `.gitignore` block is one line, `/.rvenv/`.

`rvenv.cfg` is the `pyvenv.cfg` analog: R packages are ABI-tied to R minor
version + platform + arch, and activation validates this and a mismatch is
a hard error.

### Three activation layers, no project `.Rprofile`

1. **Process activation (shell use).**

   `.rvenv/bin/R` is a wrapper script (not a symlink) that exports
   `R_LIBS_USER`, clears `R_LIBS`, points `R_LIBS_SITE` at a nonexistent
   path, sets `R_REPOSITORIES` at a venv-owned repositories file, then
   execs the real R by absolute path. A symlink alone would resolve
   `R_HOME` correctly but carry no environment, letting the user level
   package library leak in. The wrapper also pins the exact R the venv was
   built against.

   `.rvenv/bin/activate` (with `activate.fish`, `activate.csh`, and
   `Activate.ps1` variants) is the sourced-shell alternative to the
   wrapper: it exports the same environment variables into the current
   shell and prepends `.rvenv/bin` to `PATH`, so plain `R`/`Rscript`
   resolve to the venv without invoking the wrapper explicitly.

2. **Implicit activation (scripts/CI), `rig run`.**

   `rig run script.R` walks up from the working directory, finds `.rvenv`,
   syncs it if stale, and execs with the right environment, no sourcing, no
   shell state, correct in CI and Makefiles. This is the intended default,
   `activate` is the compatibility path for interactive shells.

3. **In-session activation (IDEs).**

   IDEs start R directly, with no wrapper and no `PATH` interception
   available. Instead of a project `.Rprofile` (rejected, since it causes
   issues for renv), this proposal uses a tracked project `.Renviron` file
   plus a small R package, `rvenv`, loaded via `R_DEFAULT_PACKAGES`:

    ```
    # .Renviron (tracked, relative paths)
    RVENV_R_LIBS_USER=${R_LIBS_USER}
    R_LIBS_USER=.rvenvlib
    R_DEFAULT_PACKAGES=rvenv,datasets,utils,grDevices,graphics,stats,methods
    ```

   This works because R reads `.Renviron` before it reads `Rprofile.site`
   or `.Rprofile`, so `R_LIBS_USER` is set before any package is loaded,
   and the shim package is loaded first, before any other package.

   `R_LIBS_USER` here names the venv's own library, `.rvenvlib`, not
   the project library: it only has to get R far enough to load the shim
   package, which is the one library that is guaranteed to be there in a
   fresh clone. Pointing R at the project library is the shim's job.
   `RVENV_R_LIBS_USER` records the value the R installation had set, before
   `.Renviron` overwrites it, for the not-yet-synced case below.

   Starting R with `--vanilla` or `--no-environ`, or setting
   `R_ENVIRON_USER` to point elsewhere, skips reading `.Renviron`
   entirely, so this in-session activation does not run. This is a known
   escape hatch, not a bug: those flags exist to bypass environment/profile
   setup, and a user reaching for them intends to opt out.

   The shim package's `.onLoad` is split across two files, so that fixes to
   the activation logic reach already-`init`'ed projects on their next
   `sync`, with no `rig proj init` or `rig` upgrade required:

   - `.onLoad` itself, in the committed shim package, always restores the
     user's real `~/.Renviron` first (un-shadowing it). It is otherwise kept
     to the one thing that has to work even before a project has ever been
     synced: if `.rvenv/lib` does not exist yet, there is nothing to
     activate, and leaving `R_LIBS_USER` at `.rvenvlib` would leave the
     session with rig's own directory as its user library, so
     `install.packages()` would write there. So it restores `R_LIBS_USER`
     and `.libPaths()` to what a session outside the project would have
     had, using the recorded `RVENV_R_LIBS_USER` (expanded with R's own
     `%`-spec expander, since `.Renviron` files are read before R expands
     those), and only prints the sync reminder.
   - If `.rvenv/lib` does exist, `.onLoad` `source()`s `.rvenv/onload.R`,
     which `sync` writes fresh every time, `local = TRUE` so it runs in
     `.onLoad`'s own frame and reuses its locals. This is where the rest of
     activation lives: it backs off the same way as an unsynced project (an
     R-version mismatch between the project library and the running R is
     treated as binary-incompatible, not merely stale), otherwise sets
     `R_LIBS_USER` to the project library, `.rvenv/lib`, as an absolute
     path, via `Sys.setenv()` (not `options()`, since `options()` set
     inside `.onLoad` does not propagate to children), appends the shared
     dev-tool library (`tools-lib` in `rvenv.cfg`, resolved once by `sync`,
     not derived by the shim itself, since by the time R starts under
     `rig run`'s wrapper the R installation's own default user library is
     already gone), makes the result `.libPaths()[1]`, and prints a
     "venv not synced" message if the lock file's copy in
     `.rvenv/lib/.synced` does not match `rproj.lock`. Resolving the
     project library's path to an absolute one is what makes child
     processes started from a subdirectory (callr, parallel, `R CMD`,
     `Rscript`) use the same library: they inherit the environment
     variable, not the shim's `.libPaths()` call.

   The shim package must be **there on a fresh clone**, before anything is
   installed: if `R_DEFAULT_PACKAGES=rvenv,...` names a package that does
   not exist, R prints its own unhelpful "package ... was not found"
   warning instead of the friendly sync reminder, with no way to intercept
   it. So `rig proj init` writes it into `.rvenvlib/rvenv` and it is
   committed, rather than `sync` installing it.

   `init` writes it *without running R*: the project's R may not be
   installed yet, and it may be an R that rig does not manage. So the shim
   is a **fake installed package**, a directory that looks like the result
   of `R CMD INSTALL` but is only files embedded in the `rig` binary:
   `DESCRIPTION`, `NAMESPACE`, `LICENSE`, plain `R/rvenv` source (no
   lazy-load database) and a `Meta/package.rds` generated at rig build
   time. Nothing in it is tied to an R version except two strings in
   `package.rds`, so the same committed directory loads on every R the
   project may be opened with: `Built$R` is stamped `4.0.0` (below that,
   `loadNamespace()` refuses to load the package at all), `Built$Platform`
   is empty (which is what keeps the "built for a different platform"
   check quiet on Windows), and the file is serialized in format 2, which
   R < 3.5.0 can still read. Verified to load on R 3.4.4 through 4.6.1.

### Fit with `rig`

This folds into the existing `rig proj` namespace rather than a new
`rig venv` verb, since `rig proj` already parses manifests, solves, and
deploys. A venv is that same machinery pointed at `.rvenv/lib`, plus the
activation layers above:

- `rig proj lock` writes `rproj.lock` (TOML), an array of
  per-`(R version, platform)` targets.
- `rig proj sync` reads `rproj.lock`, creates the project library
  `.rvenv/lib` and installs the matching target into it, resolving and
  installing the lock file's named R version first if it is missing.
- `rig proj init` writes the tracked part of the layout up front
  (`.Renviron`, the `.gitignore` block, the shim package in
  `.rvenvlib`).
- `rig run <file.R>` walks up from the working directory for a project,
  syncs it if stale, and runs it with `.rvenv/bin/R` instead of the default
  R, the `uv run` equivalent.

## Implementation

Support for rvenv is implemented in [`rig`](https://github.com/r-lib/rig),
version 0.10.0 (currently beta).

1. `rig proj init` writes the tracked part of the layout (the shim package
   in `.rvenvlib`), `.Renviron`, and the `.gitignore` block. The shim
   package files are embedded in the `rig` binary, so no R is needed to
   write them.
1. `rig proj sync` creating the full environment, not just the library:
   Writes `rvenv.cfg`, `onload.R` (the machine-specific rest of the shim
   package's `.onLoad()`, sourced by the committed part), `etc/repositories`,
   the `bin/R`/`bin/Rscript` wrappers, and sh/bash/zsh/csh/fish/cmd/PowerShell
   activation scripts from one shared list of environment variables.

   On Windows `rig proj sync` creates `.exe`-shims that carry the
   environment variables and the path of the required R version.
1. `rig run` uses the project environment.

## Backwards compatibility

This is the first version of `.rvenv`, so there is no backwards
compatibility to maintain.

`rig proj import` helps with migrating existing renv and `DESCRIPTION`
based projects into `.rvenv`.

## How to teach

`rig proj init` would be taught as the equivalent of
`python -m venv`/`uv venv`, and `rig run`/`rig proj sync` as the equivalent
of `uv run`/`uv sync`. The three activation layers should be taught in
order of preference: `rig run` and other implicit, non-interactive uses
first (no shell state to manage, correct in CI), the shell wrapper
(`source .rvenv/bin/activate`) second for interactive use, and the IDE
`.Renviron`/shim mechanism documented separately as "how IDEs pick this up
automatically," since most users will never need to think about it
directly.
